source_text: hac conscientia instructi aduersus opinionem ethnicorum conuertamur magis ad nostrorum detractatus. quorundam enim fides aut simplicior aut scrupulosior ad hanc abdicationem spectaculorum de scripturis auctoritatem exposcit et se in incertum constituit, quod non significanter neque nominatim denuntietur seruis dei abstinentia eiusmodi. plane nusquam inuenimus, quemadmodum aperte positum est: non occides, non idolum coles, non adulterium, non fraudem admitt es, ita exerte definitum: non ibis in circum, non in theatrum, agonem, munus non spectabis. sed inuenimus ad hanc quoque speciem pertinere illam primam uocem Dauid: felix uir, inquit, qui non abiit in concilium impiorum et in uia peccatorum non stetit nec in calthe]dra pestium sedit. nam etsi iustum illum uidetur prał\\dicaвse, quod in] concilio et in consessu Iudaeorum de necando domino consultantium non communicauit, late tamen semper scriptura diuina diuiditur, ubicumque secundum praesentis rei sensum etiam disciplina munitur, ut hic quoque non sit aliena uox a spectaculorum interdictione. si enim pauculos tunc Iudaeos impiorum concilium uocauit, quanto magis tantum conuentum ethnici populi? minus impii ethnici, minus peccatores, minus hostes Christi quam tunc Iudaei? quid quod et cetera congruunt. nam apud spectacula et in cathedra sedetur et in Uia statur; uias enim et cardines uocant balteorum per ambitum et discrimina popularium per procliuum; cathedra quoque nominatur. ipse in anfractu ad consessum situs. itaque e contrario \'inf felix qui in quodcumque concilium impiorum abierit et in quacumque uia peccatorum steterit et in quacumque cathedra pestium sederit\' generaliter dictum intellegamus. cum quid aliud, etiam specialiter interpretari capit. nam et specialiter quaedam pronuntiata generaliter sapiunt. cum deus Israhelitas admonet disciplinae uel obiurgat, utique ad omnes habet; cum Aegypto et Aethiopiae exitium comminatur, utique in omnem gentem peccatricem praeiudicat.
orientation: Tertullian is answering Christians who want an explicit scriptural prohibition of the shows, and he turns to Psalm 1 as a broad principle that covers them.
pass_a_gloss: Instructed by this conscience against the opinion of the pagans, let us turn rather to the disparagements of our own people. For the faith of some, either more simple or more scrupulous, demands from the Scriptures authority for this renunciation of shows, and places itself in uncertainty, because abstinence of this kind is not expressly and by name denounced to the servants of God. Clearly nowhere do we find, just as it is openly set down: you shall not kill, you shall not worship an idol, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not admit fraud, so explicitly defined: you shall not go into the circus, not into the theater, you shall not watch a contest, a gladiatorial show. But we find that that first voice of David also pertains to this kind: happy is the man, he says, who has not gone into the council of the impious and has not stood in the way of sinners and has not sat in the chair of pestilences. For even if he seems to have proclaimed that just man, because he did not share in the council and in the assembly of the Jews who were plotting to kill the Lord, yet the divine Scripture is always divided broadly, wherever according to the sense of the present matter discipline is also fortified, so that here too the voice is not foreign to the prohibition of shows. For if he called the few Jews of that time a council of the impious, how much more the great assembly of the pagan people? Are the pagans less impious, less sinners, less enemies of Christ than the Jews of that time? What of the fact that the other things also agree? For at the shows one both sits in a chair and stands in a way; for they call the ways and hinges of the baltei through the circuit and the divisions of the people through the slope; it is also called a chair, the very seat placed in the curve for sitting. Therefore on the contrary let us understand as said generally: unhappy is he who has gone into any council of the impious and has stood in any way of sinners and has sat in any chair of pestilences. Since what else, it also begins to be interpreted specially. For some things pronounced specially also have a general sense. When God admonishes the Israelites for discipline or rebukes them, he certainly addresses all; when he threatens destruction to Egypt and Ethiopia, he certainly judges beforehand against every sinful nation.

choices.why: The glossary fixes 'renunciation' for renuntiatio; abdicatio here is a synonym, and 'shows' is the fixed rendering for spectacula.
The source has OCR damage (calthe]dra); the lemma is cathedra, and 'chair' preserves the literal furniture image Tertullian exploits.
Literal rendering of the Psalm phrase; 'council' keeps the deliberative assembly sense Tertullian applies to the crowd at shows.
Literal rendering of the Psalm phrase; 'way' is needed because Tertullian later connects it to the physical walkways (uiae) in the circus.
The term is a technical circus word for the walkways or tiers; keeping it transliterated preserves the technical sense Tertullian is explaining.
The verb means to decide in advance or establish a precedent; 'judges beforehand' captures the legal force of God's threat as a standing judgment.

pass_b_english: Armed with this knowledge against the opinions of pagans, let us turn instead to the objections of our own people. For some of them, whose faith is either too simple or too scrupulous, demand scriptural authority for giving up shows, and they place themselves in uncertainty because abstinence of this kind is not denounced to God's servants specifically and by name.

Of course we nowhere find it laid down as openly as "You shall not kill, you shall not worship an idol, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not commit fraud" (Exodus 20:13-15), so explicitly defined: "You shall not go into the circus, you shall not go into the theater, you shall not watch a contest or a gladiatorial show."

But we do find that the first voice of David applies to this very category: "Blessed is the man," he says, "who has not gone into the council of the impious, and has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the chair of ruin" (Psalm 1:1). For even if he seems to have proclaimed that righteous man blessed because he did not share in the council and assembly of the Jews who were plotting the death of the Lord, divine Scripture is nevertheless always applied broadly: wherever discipline is also strengthened according to the sense of the present matter, so that here too the voice is not foreign to the prohibition of shows.

For if David called a few Jews of that time a council of the impious, how much more is the vast assembly of the pagan people such a council? Are pagans less impious, less sinners, less enemies of Christ than the Jews of that time were? What of the fact that the other details also fit? For at the shows people sit in a chair and stand in a way; they call the walkways and the dividing barriers around the circuit and the separations of the common people along the slope "ways," and the place itself in the curve for sitting is also called a "chair."

Therefore let us understand the reverse statement as spoken generally: "Unhappy is he who has gone into any council of the impious, and has stood in any way of sinners, and has sat in any chair of ruin." Since it can also be interpreted specifically, it certainly admits of that. For certain pronouncements made specifically also have a general sense. When God admonishes the Israelites for discipline or rebukes them, he certainly addresses everyone; when he threatens destruction to Egypt and Ethiopia, he certainly judges beforehand against every sinful nation.

polish.changed: Clarified the objector's voice, replaced opaque phrases like 'divided broadly' and 'fortified' with natural equivalents, translated 'baltei' as 'dividing barriers,' rendered 'pestilences' as 'ruin' per the reader note, and smoothed sentence rhythm for reading aloud.

notes.quote: Of course we nowhere find it laid down as openly
notes.why: Christian objector's voice blends with author's.

notes.quote: divine Scripture is nevertheless always divided broadly: wherever discipline is also fortified according to the sense of the present matter
notes.why: 'Divided broadly' and 'fortified' are opaque; meaning unclear.
notes.fix: Revise to 'Scripture speaks generally, applicable to many cases'.

notes.quote: the walkways and divisions of the baltei around the circuit
notes.why: 'baltei' (Latin for the dividing barriers in a circus) is untranslated and obscure.
notes.fix: Translate as 'barriers' or 'low walls' instead of leaving Latin 'baltei.'

notes.why: 'Pestilences' for Latin 'pestis' likely means 'ruin' or 'destruction,' not disease.
notes.fix: Render as 'the seat of destruction' or 'the chair of ruin.'

polish.changed: Clarified who is speaking (David), unified the term for giving up shows, and smoothed sentence flow for reading aloud while preserving every claim and Scripture reference.

notes.why: Multiple terms for the same concept of giving up shows; reader may think different things are meant.
notes.fix: Use 'renunciation of shows' consistently or note synonyms.

notes.why: Latin 'munus' introduced as etymology but then the show is called by different names; reader may lose the connection.
notes.fix: Note that munus = gladiatorial show throughout.
